title: Why is multi-level rate limiting (per-user vs per-IP vs per-provider vs global) more effective than a single limiter, and why must per-provider limits use a token bucket per downstream so you can fail over cleanly when one provider's bucket is empty rather than hammering a rate-limited provider?
shortTitle: Why is multi-level rate limiting more effective than a single limiter, and why a token bucket per downstream provider
keyPoints: Each rate-limiting scope catches a different abuse pattern that others are blind to.
Per-user stops one account monopolizing capacity; per-IP catches one source attacking many accounts.
Per-provider keeps outbound calls within a downstream's contractual rate; global protects total system capacity.
A single limiter at any scope has blind spots that other scopes cover, so you compose all levels.
A token bucket per provider tracks each downstream's remaining allowance independently.
When one provider's bucket empties, you fail over to a provider that still has tokens instead of hammering the exhausted one.
Hammering a rate-limited provider wastes threads, triggers penalties, and can create a feedback loop.

s1_definition.oneliner: Multi-level rate limiting works because per-user, per-IP, per-provider, and global each catch a distinct pattern, and a token bucket per provider enables clean failover instead of hammering an exhausted provider.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Multi-level rate limiting** – Separate limits at per-user, per-IP, per-provider, and global scopes, evaluated together.
- **Per-user** – Stops one account monopolizing capacity (e.g., 5 OTPs/min per user).
- **Per-IP** – Catches one source attacking many accounts (e.g., credential stuffing from one IP).
- **Per-provider** – Keeps outbound calls within a downstream's contractual rate.
- **Global** – Protects total system capacity from any flood larger than you can serve.
- **Token bucket per provider** – Tracks each downstream's remaining allowance so you fail over to one with tokens.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India controlling a crowd at a service hall. One rule cannot stop a greedy customer, spot a troublemaker using many names, and respect each printer's speed limit. So the bank uses several rules: no single customer gets too many, no single entrance lets too many through, each printer is asked to print only as fast as it can, and the whole hall has a cap. When one printer's quota is used up, the clerk sends the next job to a printer that still has quota.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Multi-Level Rate Limiting:

  Request
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  FAIL
  │ Per-User     │──────▶ 429 Too Many Requests
  │ 5/min/acct   │
  └──────┬───────┘
    PASS │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  FAIL
  │ Per-IP       │──────▶ 429 + CAPTCHA
  │ 20/min/IP    │
  └──────┬───────┘
    PASS │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  FAIL
  │ Per-Provider │──────▶ Fail over to next provider
  │ token bucket │
  └──────┬───────┘
    PASS │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  FAIL
  │ Global       │──────▶ 503 Service Unavailable
  │ 10000/sec    │
  └──────┬───────┘
    PASS │
    ▼
  Process Request

  Per-Provider Failover:
  ┌────────────┐  empty  ┌────────────┐  has tokens
  │ Twilio     │────────▶│ MSG91      │──────────▶ Send
  │ bucket: 0  │         │ bucket: 45 │
  └────────────┘         └────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Multi-level rate limiting beats a single limiter because each scope catches a pattern the others are blind to. Per-user stops one account monopolizing. Per-IP catches one source attacking many accounts. Per-provider keeps outbound calls within a downstream's rate. Global protects total capacity. Removing any one opens a specific hole, so you compose all levels.

The per-provider limit must be a token bucket per downstream because it tracks each provider's remaining allowance independently. When one provider's bucket empties, you immediately route to one that still has tokens instead of hammering the exhausted provider. Hammering wastes threads, triggers penalties, and can create a feedback loop. The bucket complements a circuit breaker: the bucket handles rate limits, the breaker handles errors.

At National Bank of India, a single global limiter on OTP sending failed both ways: an abusive script spread across many accounts slipped under, and lowering the threshold throttled real customers. Pankaj moved to layered limits with per-user, per-IP, global, and a token bucket per SMS provider in Redis. When the primary provider's bucket emptied, the router failed over to the secondary cleanly.

Remember one sentence: multi-level rate limiting composes per-user, per-IP, per-provider, and global scopes because each catches patterns the others miss, and a token bucket per provider enables clean failover to one with tokens instead of hammering an exhausted provider.
